invariant_bindings.invariant_text: Subject names MUST NOT contain null, whitespace, '.', '*' or '>' inside a token because these are the reserved separators.
The '>' wildcard SHALL appear only as the final token of a pattern and match one or more remaining tokens.
The '*' wildcard MUST match exactly one token, never zero and never multiple.
Names starting with '$' are FORBIDDEN for user subjects because that prefix is reserved for system use.
Publishers ALWAYS send to a fully specified subject; wildcards CANNOT appear in a publish call.

tier_reports.summary: mypy --strict clean; ruff (curated ALL) clean; 1 suppressions all rationale-attached.
LLM judge ≥8/10 on six axes; all five personas understood the docs.

attacks.hypothesis: The '>' wildcard should match one or more tokens, but matches() returns True when '>' has zero remaining tokens (i == len(name_tokens)), violating the one-or-more requirement.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject('a.b').matches('a.b.>') returns True but should be False

attacks.hypothesis: The matches() function does not enforce that '>' appears only as final token. A pattern like 'a.>.c' is silently accepted and short-circuits at '>', ignoring trailing tokens entirely.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject('a.x.y.z').matches('a.>.c') returns True, ignoring the illegal trailing '.c'

attacks.hypothesis: '*' is supposed to match exactly one non-empty token, but split('.') produces empty strings for consecutive dots, so '*' will match an empty token, violating the one-token-never-zero rule.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject('a..b').matches('a.*.b') returns True even though middle token is empty

attacks.hypothesis: Constructor accepts names with embedded dots, violating the reserved-separator invariant. No validation is performed in __init__, so a name like 'a..b' or 'foo.bar' is accepted as a single StreamSubject.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='order.created.v1') treated as single subject but split yields multiple tokens

attacks.hypothesis: Constructor accepts whitespace, tab, and newline characters within names without validation, breaking the reserved-character invariant and enabling subject spoofing where 'order ' visually equals 'order'.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='order\ncreated') and StreamSubject(name=' order') both accepted

attacks.hypothesis: No validation rejects the null byte (\x00) in names, violating the reserved-character invariant and potentially enabling C-string truncation attacks in downstream consumers.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='order\x00admin') is constructed without error

attacks.hypothesis: The '$' prefix is reserved for system subjects but the constructor performs zero validation, allowing user code to forge system subjects like '$SYS.account' and impersonate internal events.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='$SYS.ACCOUNT.CONNECT') constructs successfully

attacks.hypothesis: Constructor accepts '*' or '>' as part of a name token, allowing a publisher to construct StreamSubject('a.>') or StreamSubject('*.b'), violating the publisher-no-wildcards invariant at the type boundary.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='orders.>') is accepted and would publish to a wildcard

attacks.hypothesis: StreamSubject(name='') is accepted; split('.') yields ['']; matching against '*' would match an empty token, and '>' would match zero tokens, breaking multiple invariants simultaneously.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='').matches('*') returns True

attacks.hypothesis: A trailing dot in name like 'orders.' splits to ['orders',''] producing a phantom empty token that '*' matches, allowing pattern 'orders.*' to spuriously match a malformed subject.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='orders.').matches('orders.*') returns True

attacks.hypothesis: A consumer pattern starting with '>' alone matches every subject, including reserved '$SYS.*' system subjects, allowing privilege escalation by user consumers subscribing to system streams.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='$SYS.ACCOUNT.X').matches('>') returns True

attacks.hypothesis: matches() performs no type validation on pattern argument; passing a non-string (None, int, bytes) raises AttributeError instead of a controlled validation error, leaking implementation details and crashing consumer dispatch loops.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='a.b').matches(None) raises AttributeError

attacks.hypothesis: matches() has no bound on token count; an attacker-controlled subject of 1M dot-separated tokens forces split() and an O(n) loop per consumer, enabling CPU amplification DoS across all subscribers.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='a.'*1_000_000 + 'b').matches('>')

attacks.hypothesis: Despite frozen=True, the underlying str is interned and equality is structural; an attacker can construct two StreamSubjects with visually identical names using Unicode homoglyphs (e.g., Cyrillic 'о' vs Latin 'o') to bypass ACL checks keyed on subject equality.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='\u043erder.created') vs StreamSubject(name='order.created')

attacks.hypothesis: The '>' wildcard is supposed to match ONE OR MORE remaining tokens, but the condition `i <= len(name_tokens)` is an off-by-one: when `i == len(name_tokens)` there are exactly zero tokens left to consume, yet the expression evaluates True. Concretely, StreamSubject(name='a').matches('a.>') returns True even though no tokens follow 'a', violating the 'one or more' guarantee of the '>' invariant.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='a').matches('a.>') → True  # WRONG: should be False, zero tokens after 'a'

attacks.hypothesis: The '>' token is supposed to appear ONLY as the final token, but the implementation never enforces position. A pattern like 'a.>.b' would hit the '>' branch at i=1, evaluate `1 <= len(name_tokens)`, and return True immediately without inspecting the remaining 'b' token. This lets an attacker craft patterns that skip required suffix segments and match subjects they should not.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='a.x.y').matches('a.>.b') → True  # WRONG: '>' is not last token, and 'b' suffix is ignored

attacks.hypothesis: The frozen dataclass performs zero validation on the 'name' field, so nothing prevents constructing StreamSubject(name='foo.*bar') or StreamSubject(name='foo.a>b'). A token embedding '*' or '>' mid-token violates the reserved-separator invariant. When this name is later used as a filter pattern it will be split on '.' and the embedded wildcard character will silently influence matching in unpredictable ways.
attacks.input_fixture: s = StreamSubject(name='foo.*bar'); s.matches('foo.*bar') → True  # name constructed with embedded wildcard, no rejection

attacks.hypothesis: The '*' wildcard must match exactly one token and never zero. But 'exactly one' implies a non-empty token. When a name contains a double-dot ('a..b'), split('.') yields an empty string '' as the middle token. The '*' branch only checks tok != '*', not that the matched name token is non-empty, so '*' silently matches the zero-length token, effectively matching zero meaningful characters and violating the 'never zero' half of the invariant.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='a..b').matches('a.*.b') → True  # '*' matched empty string token at position 1

attacks.hypothesis: The invariant forbids user subjects whose names start with '$' because that prefix is reserved for system subjects. The frozen dataclass performs no such check, allowing StreamSubject(name='$SYS.services.status') to be constructed silently. An agent publishing to or subscribing with this subject can hijack system-reserved routing channels without any error being raised.
attacks.input_fixture: s = StreamSubject(name='$SYS.services.status'); assert s.name.startswith('$')  # constructed without error

attacks.hypothesis: Publishers must always send to a fully specified subject; wildcards must not appear in a publish-side name. However, nothing in the API prevents constructing StreamSubject(name='orders.*.created') and calling matches() on it (using the wildcard-bearing subject as if it were a legitimate publish target). Because the dataclass accepts any string, a buggy publisher could silently route through a wildcard name and the code would accept it.
attacks.input_fixture: pub = StreamSubject(name='orders.*.created'); pub.matches('orders.*.created') → True  # wildcard name accepted as publisher subject

attacks.hypothesis: The reserved-character list explicitly includes the null character. The dataclass does not strip or reject null bytes, so StreamSubject(name='foo\x00bar') is constructed cleanly. Downstream systems (logging, serialization, C-extension NATS clients) that treat '\x00' as a string terminator would truncate the subject to 'foo', silently changing the routing key while the Python layer believes the full name was transmitted.
attacks.input_fixture: s = StreamSubject(name='foo\x00bar.baz'); assert s.name == 'foo\x00bar.baz'  # null byte stored with no rejection

attacks.hypothesis: Whitespace is explicitly listed as a reserved/forbidden character inside a token. The dataclass applies no strip or validation, so StreamSubject(name='user events.created') can be constructed. When this name is later compared against a pattern in matches(), the whitespace-bearing token must match a literal whitespace pattern token, creating an invisible differentiation that is trivially misconfigured by operators and violates the invariant.
attacks.input_fixture: s = StreamSubject(name='user events.created'); s.matches('user events.created') → True  # whitespace in token accepted silently

attacks.hypothesis: A name with a trailing dot ('foo.bar.') produces a trailing empty string token when split on '.'. The '*' wildcard at that position will match the empty string, making StreamSubject(name='foo.bar.').matches('foo.bar.*') return True. This lets a malformed subject slip through consumer filters that were only intended to match well-formed three-token names, potentially routing garbage into consumer handlers.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='foo.bar.').matches('foo.bar.*') → True  # trailing empty token matched by '*'

attacks.hypothesis: StreamSubject(name='') is constructable. Calling split('.') on '' returns [''], a list of length 1 containing one empty-string token. A pattern of '>' then hits `i=0, tok='>'` and evaluates `0 <= 1` → True, so the empty subject matches the catch-all wildcard. Worse, a pattern of '*' also matches because len(['']) == len(['*']) == 1 and the '*' branch does not reject an empty token. An empty subject should be invalid but instead silently routes through every wildcard consumer.
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='').matches('>') → True; StreamSubject(name='').matches('*') → True  # empty name accepted and matches catch-all

attacks.hypothesis: The matches() method splits both name and pattern on '.' and then iterates token-by-token. An attacker or misconfigured publisher can construct a subject with 100 000 dot-separated tokens (e.g. 'a.' * 100000 + 'b'). Each call to matches() allocates two lists of 100 000 strings and iterates the full length. A single broker process calling matches() across N active subscriptions would exhibit O(depth × subscriptions) CPU and memory growth, enabling a denial-of-service amplification attack with no built-in depth limit.
attacks.input_fixture: deep = 'a.' * 100000 + 'b'; s = StreamSubject(name=deep); s.matches(deep)  # 200 000 token allocations, no depth cap

attacks.hypothesis: The implementation splits on the ASCII period '\u002E' only. Unicode contains visually identical characters such as the one-dot leader '\u2024' and the fullwidth full stop '\uFF0E'. A subject like StreamSubject(name='foo\u2024bar') stores a single unsplit token containing what looks like a dot. Pattern matching against 'foo.bar' fails (correctly), but a mis-configured subscription using the same Unicode dot as a literal separator would bypass the routing check entirely, violating the reserved-separator invariant which only lists the ASCII period.
attacks.input_fixture: s = StreamSubject(name='foo\u2024bar'); s.matches('foo.bar') → False  # Unicode lookalike bypasses ASCII-only split, token not separated

attacks.hypothesis: StreamSubject constructor does not validate input; name can contain null bytes, whitespace, or reserved separators inside tokens, violating the reserved character invariant
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='foo\x00bar'); StreamSubject(name='foo bar.baz'); StreamSubject(name='foo\nbar')

attacks.hypothesis: StreamSubject constructor accepts '*' and '>' characters in subject names, violating the publisher contract that subjects must be fully specified without wildcards
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='foo.*.bar'); StreamSubject(name='user.>.event')

attacks.hypothesis: StreamSubject does not enforce the $ prefix reservation; user code can create system subjects, breaking isolation contract
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='$internal.metrics'); StreamSubject(name='$__reserved__')

attacks.hypothesis: Double dots or leading/trailing dots create empty string tokens; empty tokens violate the non-empty character rule and produce unexpected match behavior
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='foo..bar').matches('foo.*.bar'); StreamSubject(name='.foo.bar'); StreamSubject(name='foo.bar.')

attacks.hypothesis: Pattern 'a.>' against name 'a' returns True when '>' should match one or more remaining tokens; condition uses <= instead of < allowing zero remaining tokens
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='a').matches('a.>') evaluates to True; should require at least one token after 'a'

attacks.hypothesis: Pattern with '>' in middle position returns immediately without validating remaining pattern tokens, e.g., 'a.>.b' ignores the final 'b' token requirement
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='a.x.y').matches('a.>.b') returns True; should fail because final token is 'b', not checked

attacks.hypothesis: Pattern '*' against empty name '' should fail (asterisk requires exactly one token) but may incorrectly succeed due to boundary condition in loop
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='').matches('*') or StreamSubject(name='').matches('a.*')

attacks.hypothesis: Empty string subject names are not rejected; creates degenerate token list and undefined match behavior for patterns like '' or '>'
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name=''); then call .matches('') or .matches('*') or .matches('>')

attacks.hypothesis: Pattern strings containing null bytes are not sanitized before split, producing malformed token lists that may bypass match validation
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='a.b').matches('a\x00b.c') or StreamSubject(name='a').matches('a.\x00>')

attacks.hypothesis: Subject names with embedded whitespace are accepted; patterns with spaces create tokens that never match literals, causing silent false negatives
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='user create.event').matches('user create.*') vs StreamSubject(name='user create.event').matches('user.create.*')

attacks.hypothesis: Pattern consisting of sole '>' token matches any non-empty subject; violates the invariant that '>' should only appear as final token with preceding context
attacks.input_fixture: StreamSubject(name='a.b.c').matches('>') or StreamSubject(name='x').matches('>')

attacks.hypothesis: Although StreamSubject is frozen, if mutable name string is stored and later mutated externally (e.g., via ctypes), matches() behavior becomes non-deterministic across calls
attacks.input_fixture: Create StreamSubject, externally mutate internal string, call matches() twice and compare results

axes.rationale: Implementation matches all five declared invariants; matches() follows SS_INV_02 'one or more remaining' via `i < len(name_tokens)`, SS_INV_03 via strict length equality when no '>', SS_INV_04/05 enforced at construction.
Exposes StreamSubject, SubjectRegistry, dedicated error, both validators, and all constants. Covers publish/subscribe/unsubscribe/deliveries and all 5 SS_INV_* rules. No obvious gap versus spec.

StreamSubjectError subclasses ValueError; every raise cites the specific SS_INV_* ID, includes offending token/name via repr, and distinguishes wildcard-in-publish vs reserved-char vs system-prefix cases.
Frozen dataclass value type, pure free-function validators reusable outside the class, registry is an optional stateful companion not required by the primitive, clean __all__, zero import-time I/O.

Thread-safe registry via Lock, immutable subject, lazy state. Minor concerns: _delivered list grows unbounded (no cap/rotation), publish re-validates pattern via matches() inside the lock on every fan-out (redundant since subscribe already validated), no metrics hooks despite spec mentioning self-observability.

Protocol shape (frozen dataclass, name:str, matches(pattern)->bool) matches catalog. Semantic tightening vs catalog api_signature: catalog sketch uses `i <= len(name_tokens)` for '>' (permits zero trailing), impl uses `i < len(name_tokens)` to honor SS_INV_02's 'one or more' — aligns with invariant text but diverges from the sketch.

friction_points: 'fan-out', 'broker subjects', 'consumer routing predicates' are used before being defined — the plain-language intro doesn't resolve them.
EventEnvelope is referenced in 'When NOT to use' with no link or explanation of what it is.
The TLA+/TLC sentence in 'Formal model' reads as jargon noise — a junior dev won't know whether to care or skip it.
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Lead 'When to use' with a one-sentence analogy ('think of it like a file path that filters which listeners receive a message'), hyperlink EventEnvelope, and move the TLA+ sentence to an 'Advanced / formal verification' collapsible section.

friction_points: 'implementing a naming convention validator that wraps the constructor' — no interface signature or ABC shown; extension contract is hand-wavy.
StreamSubject.contract.json is referenced but not excerpted; it's unclear whether it's a JSON Schema, AsyncAPI fragment, or something proprietary.
No mention of serialization: can a StreamSubject round-trip through JSON/msgpack cleanly, and does the frozen dataclass expose __str__/__repr__ for wire use?
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Add a 3-line ABC stub for the naming-convention validator, note the contract.json schema dialect (JSON Schema draft-07?), and add a one-liner on str() output format for wire serialization.

friction_points: Enforcement locus is ambiguous: is the '$' prefix check and char-class validation done client-side only, or also enforced at the broker? A rogue client bypassing the SDK breaks the guarantee.
No mention of subject-enumeration risk: a subscriber with pattern '>' can observe all subjects; doc is silent on whether that requires elevated ACLs.
No rejection audit log — rejected subjects (null bytes, $ prefix) silently fail or raise? No guidance on whether to alert on rejection spikes.
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Add a 'Trust boundary' row to the Security section stating where validation is authoritative (client + broker dual enforcement or client-only), note that '>' subscriptions require ACL review, and specify whether ValidationError is raised or logged on rejection.

friction_points: Metric paths ('subject.publications.total', 'subject.fanout.size') look like NATS stat paths, not Prometheus metric names — unclear how to scrape or alert on them.
SubjectRegistry has no documented max-size or eviction policy; unbounded growth under subscription churn is a memory-leak risk with no operational mitigation stated.
p99 < 1µs claim has no benchmark methodology attached — hardware, token length, registry size — making it impossible to validate in a specific deployment.
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Add a Prometheus metric name table mapping each stat to its exported name and type, add a 'Registry limits' note (max subscriptions, eviction behavior), and link or describe the benchmark harness behind the p99 claim.

friction_points: No business motivation: the doc never says what product problem this solves or why centralising subject routing matters for multi-tenant isolation at the product level.
Alternatives section is purely technical; a PM needs to understand the user-facing tradeoff ('regex routing would let teams define richer rules but doubles routing latency and removes auditability').
No adoption guidance: how much effort to integrate for a team already using plain-string topics? One-line swap or migration sprint?
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Prepend a 'Why this exists' paragraph ('before StreamSubject, every service team duplicated fan-out logic with inconsistent tenant isolation'), reframe the alternatives section with a user-facing cost sentence, and add an estimated integration size (e.g., 'drop-in for new streams; existing plain-string topics migrate with a one-line constructor wrap').
